## Introduction and data used

We illustrate in this post the notion of **ROC curves** and **Precision-Recall curves** using both simple distributions (like Gaussian or uniform) but also data from a head-to-head benchmark evaluation of five SARS-CoV-2 serological assays [@ainsworth2020performance].

For the empirical part, the underlying study compared the Abbott, DiaSorin, Oxford, Roche, and Siemens
assays using a common set of well-characterized samples.
We follow @ainsworth2020performance and have used a dataset that contains two groups of samples:

- **976 pre-pandemic samples**, used as the known-negative reference group;
- **536 laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2-positive samples**, collected at least 20 days after symptom onset.

These groups contain a total of

$$
n = 976 + 536 = 1512
$$

observations. The proportion of positive samples in this dataset is therefore

$$
\widehat{\pi}_1 = \frac{536}{1512} \approx 0.355,
$$

or approximately $35.5\%$.

**An important distinction:** this proportion describes the composition of the dataset, not necessarily the prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the population where a diagnostic test would be used. The sample composition may reflect how the study was designed and how samples were selected.

This distinction will become important when interpreting precision–recall curves and average precision, which depend on the prevalence of positive cases.

The dataset (`supplementary_dataset2.csv`) is available
[here](https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Dataset_Head-to-head_benchmark_evaluation_of_the_sensitivity_and_specificity_of_five_immunoassays_for_SARS-CoV-2_serology_on_1500_samples/12622172).
The supplementary material of the associated paper describes the preprocessing used in this analysis.


## Diagnostic testing as hypothesis testing

A diagnostic test can be framed as a classical **statistical hypothesis test**. In this medical context, we consider the null hypothesis
$$
\mathcal{H}_0: \text{``you are healthy''} \quad \text{(until proved otherwise)},
$$
against the alternative:
$$
\mathcal{H}_1: \text{``you are sick''} \quad \text{(here, infected by Covid-19)}.
$$

The presumption of health plays the same role as the *presumption of innocence* in a courtroom: we only reject $\mathcal{H}_0$ (*i.e.,* declare someone positive) when the evidence (here the assay result) is strong enough. Let $Y \in \{0,1\}$ denote the true health status, with $Y=0$ under $\mathcal{H}_0$ (healthy) and $Y=1$ under $\mathcal{H}_1$ (sick). In practice, declaring someone positive means the measured antibody level, modeled by a random variable $X$, must cross an assay-specific diagnostic threshold (cut-off) $t$. The resulting decision rule, our estimate of $Y$ at threshold $t$, is written $\hat{Y}_t$:

$$
\hat{Y}_t = \hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}=
\begin{cases}
1, & X \geq t,\\
0, & X < t .
\end{cases}
$$

It is convenient to isolate the two conditional laws of $X$ given the health status. Under $\mathcal H_0$, $X$ follows $\mathcal L(X\mid Y=0)$; under $\mathcal H_1$, it follows $\mathcal L(X\mid Y=1)$. We write
$$
X_0 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=0), \qquad X_1 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=1)
$$
for two independent random variables with these laws. This turns any probability conditional on $Y$ into an ordinary, unconditional probability: for every threshold $t$,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbb P(X \ge t \mid Y=0) 
& = \mathbb P(X_0\ge t),
\\
\mathbb P(X \ge t \mid Y=1) 
& = \mathbb P(X_1\ge t),
\end{align*}
$$
and we use the right-hand sides from here on, since they involve a single random variable rather than a conditional statement.

As in any hypothesis test, two types of errors can occur: rejecting $\mathcal{H}_0$ when it is in fact true (**Type I error**), or failing to reject it when it is in fact false (**Type II error**). In terms of $X_0$ and $X_1$:

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(\text{Type I error}) & = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_t=1 \mid Y=0) = \mathbb P(X_0\ge t),\\
\mathbb{P}(\text{Type II error}) & = \mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_t=0 \mid Y=1) = \mathbb P(X_1 < t).
\end{align*}
$$

In words: a Type I error is a **false positive** (the test flags a healthy person), while a Type II error is a **false negative** (the test misses a sick person). The threshold $t$ controls the trade-off between the two: lowering $t$ catches more true cases but triggers more false alarms, and vice versa. **ROC** and **precision/recall curves**, introduced below, are the tools used to visualize this trade-off as $t$ varies.

## Naming and key quantities

The dataset consists of $n$ observations, denoted $\{(Y_i, X_i)\}_{i=1,\dots,n}$, where $Y_i$ represents the true health status of individual $i$.


Naming follows the classical terminology (see *e.g.,* the [Wikipedia article on ROC curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic)). Given a fixed threshold, each sample falls into exactly one of the four categories below:

- **True Positive**: sick and correctly declared positive
$$\displaystyle\mathrm{TP} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=1,\ \hat{Y}_{t,i}=1\}$$

- **True Negative**: healthy and correctly declared negative
$$\displaystyle\mathrm{TN} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=0,\ \hat{Y}_{t,i}=0\}$$

- **False Positive**  (Type I error): healthy but wrongly declared positive
$$\displaystyle\mathrm{FP} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=0,\ \hat{Y}_{t,i}=1\}$$

- **False Negative** (Type II error): sick but wrongly declared negative
$$\displaystyle\mathrm{FN} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=1,\ \hat{Y}_{t,i}=0\}$$ 

From the true status $Y$, we define two population sizes:

- $n^{1}=\mathrm{P} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i = 1\} = \mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FN}$: total number of sick individuals in the study (**true positives**),
- $n^{0}=\mathrm{N} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i = 0\} = \mathrm{TN} + \mathrm{FP}$: total number of healthy individuals in the study (**true negatives**),

and, similarly, from the predicted status $\hat{Y}_t$:

- $\hat{\mathrm{P}}_t = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{\hat{Y}_{t,i} = 1\} = \mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FP}$: total number of individuals predicted sick at threshold $t$ (**predicted positive**),
- $\hat{\mathrm{N}}_t = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{\hat{Y}_{t,i} = 0\} = \mathrm{TN} + \mathrm{FN}$: total number of individuals predicted healthy at threshold $t$ (**predicted negative**).

![](images/tests.svg){fig-alt="Illustration of TP, TN, FP, FN counts on a Covid-19 test example"}

[Note]{.underline}: we will reuse the same color code below, with red for $\mathrm{N}$, blue for $\mathrm{P}$, crosses for a negative test result, and dots for a positive test result.


We also define the following rates, used throughout this post. Let $\pi_1:=\mathbb P(Y=1)$ and $\pi_0:=\mathbb P(Y=0)=1-\pi_1$ denote the class probabilities; we refer to $\pi_1$ as the **prevalence** of the disease in the population.

**The true rates.** These are probabilities of the underlying random variables — population quantities, not counts:

- $\mathrm{TPR}(t) := \mathbb{P}\!\left(\hat{Y}_t=1 \mid Y=1\right) = \mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$ (**True Positive Rate**, a.k.a. **sensitivity** or **recall**): among sick people, the proportion correctly detected,
- $\mathrm{TNR}(t) := \mathbb{P}\!\left(\hat{Y}_t=0 \mid Y=0\right) = \mathbb P(X_0< t)$ (**True Negative Rate**, a.k.a. **specificity**): among healthy people, the proportion correctly cleared,
- $\mathrm{FPR}(t) := \mathbb{P}\!\left(\hat{Y}_t=1 \mid Y=0\right) = \mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$ (**False Positive Rate**): among healthy people, the proportion wrongly flagged, exactly the Type I error probability,
- $\mathrm{Precision}(t) := \mathbb{P}\!\left(Y=1 \mid \hat{Y}_t=1\right)$: among people declared positive, the proportion actually sick.

The first three depend only on the conditional laws $X_0,X_1$. Precision does not: it also depends on the class probabilities $\pi_0,\pi_1$, and so, unlike the other three, cannot be written purely in terms of $X_0$ and $X_1$ (its exact form is given in @thm-precision-formula below).

**Estimators.** In practice $t$, $\pi_1$, and the laws of $X_0,X_1$ are unknown, and each rate above is estimated from a labeled sample $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$. With the notation defined earlier, the naive (plug-in) estimator of each rate simply replaces the expectation defining it by the corresponding empirical mean over the sample:
$$
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\mathrm P}, \\
\widehat{\mathrm{TNR}}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{TN}(t)}{\mathrm N}, \\
\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{FP}(t)}{\mathrm N}, \\
\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\hat{\mathrm P}_t}.\\
\end{align*}
$$

## The ROC curve

The **receiver operating characteristic** (ROC) curve traces its origins to signal detection theory, developed during **World War II** to enhance the precision of radar and sonar systems in distinguishing enemy signals from noise.
This framework, initially designed for military applications, laid the groundwork for quantifying the trade-off between detecting true threats and minimizing false alarms.
Over time, ROC analysis evolved into a universal tool for evaluating classification performance across fields like medicine, machine learning, and beyond.



:::: {#def-roc}

## ROC curve

For the threshold rule $\hat{Y}_t = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$ and a threshold $t \in \mathbb{R}$, the **ROC operating point** is defined as:

$$
\begin{align*}
\left(\mathrm{FPR}(t), \mathrm{TPR}(t)\right)
& = (
\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_t = 1 \! \mid \! Y=0),
\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_t = 1 \! \mid \! Y=1)
)\\
& = \bigl(\mathbb P(X_0\ge t),\ \mathbb P(X_1\ge t)\bigr),
\end{align*}
$$

where $X_0$ and $X_1$ denote random variables distributed as the conditional laws of $X$ given $Y=0$ and $Y=1$, respectively.

The **ROC curve** is the parametric curve traced by the operating point as $t$ varies over $\mathbb{R}$:

$$
\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{ROC}}
=
\{(\mathrm{FPR}(t), \mathrm{TPR}(t)) : t \in \mathbb{R}\}.
$$

::::



**Note**: Since FPR and TPR are probabilities, the ROC curve is contained in the unit square $[0,1] \times [0,1]$.



### Properties

#### Roc endpoints

:::: {#lem-roc-endpoints}

# ROC endpoints

Assume that $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite. Then, for the threshold rule $\hat Y_t(X)=\mathbb{1}\{X\ge t\}$, the ROC curve has the limiting endpoints:

$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to+\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)
=(0,0)
}
$$
and
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to-\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)
=(1,1).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-roc-endpoints')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-roc-endpoints .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-lem-roc-endpoints .proof-content}

**Step 1: limit as $t\to+\infty$.** By definition,
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t) = \mathbb P(X_0\ge t), \qquad \mathrm{TPR}(t) = \mathbb P(X_1\ge t).
$$
Since $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite, $\mathbb P(X_y\ge t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ for $y\in\{0,1\}$, giving
$$
\boxed{\lim_{t\to+\infty} \bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr) = (0,0).}
$$

**Step 2: limit as $t\to-\infty$.** Similarly, $\mathbb P(X_y\ge t)\to1$ as $t\to-\infty$ for $y\in\{0,1\}$, giving
$$
\boxed{\lim_{t\to-\infty} \bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr) = (1,1).}
$$

:::
::::

#### Extreme cases

##### ROC curve for a perfect classifier

:::: {#thm-perfect-separation}

# ROC curve for a perfect classifier

Suppose there exists a threshold $t^\star \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for $\hat{Y}_t = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$,
$$
\mathbb P(X_0 \ge t^\star) = 0, \qquad \mathbb P(X_1 \ge t^\star) = 1.
$$
Then,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star) = 0, \qquad \mathrm{TPR}(t^\star) = 1,}
$$
and the ROC curve passes through the upper-left corner $(0,1)$, in addition to the endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-perfect-separation')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-perfect-separation .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-perfect-separation .proof-content}
By definition, $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star) = \mathbb P(X_0 \ge t^\star) = 0$ and $\mathrm{TPR}(t^\star) = \mathbb P(X_1 \ge t^\star) = 1$. Thus the threshold $t^\star$ yields the operating point $(0,1)$, representing perfect discrimination.
:::
::::


##### ROC curve for an always-wrong classifier

:::: {#cor-perfect-anti-separation}

# ROC curve for an always-wrong classifier

Suppose there exists a threshold $t^\star \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for $\hat{Y}_t = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$,
$$
\mathbb P(X_0 \ge t^\star) = 1, \qquad \mathbb P(X_1 \ge t^\star) = 0.
$$
Then,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star) = 1, \qquad \mathrm{TPR}(t^\star) = 0,}
$$
and the ROC curve passes through the lower-right corner $(1,0)$, in addition to the endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('cor-perfect-anti-separation')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-cor-perfect-anti-separation .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-cor-perfect-anti-separation .proof-content}
By definition, $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star) = \mathbb P(X_0 \ge t^\star) = 1$ and $\mathrm{TPR}(t^\star) = \mathbb P(X_1 \ge t^\star) = 0$. Thus the threshold $t^\star$ yields the operating point $(1,0)$, representing perfectly inverted discrimination.
:::
::::


##### ROC curve under random guessing

:::: {#thm-random-guessing}

# ROC curve under random guessing

Suppose $X_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_1$, and consider the threshold rule $\hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$. Then, for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{FPR}(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t).}
$$
Consequently, the ROC curve lies on the diagonal line $u=v$ of the unit square.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-random-guessing')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-random-guessing .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-random-guessing .proof-content}
Since $X_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_1$, $\mathbb P(X_0 \ge t) = \mathbb P(X_1 \ge t)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, so $\mathrm{FPR}(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t)$ for all $t$, and the ROC curve coincides with the diagonal.
:::
::::

#### Monotonicity of ROC curves

A fundamental property of ROC curves, one that distinguishes them from Precision-Recall curves, is their **monotonicity**.

:::: {#thm-roc-monotonicity}

# Monotonicity of ROC curves

For the threshold rule $\hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X \ge t\}$, both $\mathrm{TPR}(\cdot)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(\cdot)$ are non-increasing in the threshold: for any $t_1, t_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ with $t_1 < t_2$,
$$
\mathrm{TPR}(t_1) \geq \mathrm{TPR}(t_2) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{FPR}(t_1) \geq \mathrm{FPR}(t_2).
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-monotonicity')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-monotonicity .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-monotonicity .proof-content}
Recall $\mathrm{TPR}(t) = \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t) = \mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t)$. Fix $t_1<t_2$: since $X\ge t_2$ implies $X\ge t_1$, the event $\{X\ge t_2\}$ is contained in $\{X\ge t_1\}$ for both $X_0$ and $X_1$. By monotonicity of probability measures,
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t_2) \le \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t_1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t_2) \le \mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t_1),
$$
i.e. $\mathrm{TPR}(t_1) \geq \mathrm{TPR}(t_2)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t_1) \geq \mathrm{FPR}(t_2)$.
:::
::::

##### Invariance of ROC curves under increasing transformations

A strictly increasing bijection does not introduce new ROC geometry: the ROC curve of $g(X)$ is identical to that of $X$, with only the threshold parametrization transformed via $t\mapsto g^{-1}(t)$.

:::: {#thm-roc-bijective-transform}

# Invariance of ROC curves under increasing transformations

Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable, with $X\mid Y=0$ and $X\mid Y=1$ atomless, and let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a strictly increasing bijection.
Writing 

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)=\mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=0),\\ \mathrm{TPR}_X(t)=\mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=1),
\end{align*}
$$
the operating characteristics of $g(X)$ are
$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{FPR}_{g(X)}(t) &= \mathrm{FPR}_X(g^{-1}(t)), \\
\mathrm{TPR}_{g(X)}(t) &= \mathrm{TPR}_X(g^{-1}(t)).
\end{aligned}
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-bijective-transform')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-bijective-transform .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-bijective-transform .proof-content}
Since $g$ is a strictly increasing bijection, so is $g^{-1}$, and the events $\{g(X)\ge t\}$ and $\{X\ge g^{-1}(t)\}$ coincide: $g(X)\ge t \iff X\ge g^{-1}(t)$. Hence, for $y\in\{0,1\}$,
$$
\mathbb P(g(X)\ge t\mid Y=y) = \mathbb P(X\ge g^{-1}(t)\mid Y=y),
$$
which, specializing to $y=0$ and $y=1$, is exactly the boxed identity. As $t$ ranges over $\mathbb R$, so does $g^{-1}(t)$, and $t\mapsto g^{-1}(t)$ is an order-preserving reparametrization of thresholds — so the ROC curve of $g(X)$ is identical to that of $X$, only traced by a relabeled threshold.
:::
::::

#### Symmetries of ROC curves

The ROC curve exhibits three nontrivial symmetries, generated by reversing the decision rule and/or swapping the class labels. Each acts as an exact affine reflection of the $(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})$ square, mostly because **the ROC curve is completely unaffected by class prevalence**.

For simplicity and throughout this section, assume $X\mid Y=0$ and $X\mid Y=1$ are **atomless**, *i.e.*,
$$
\mathbb P(X=t\mid Y=y)=0 \qquad \text{for every } t\in\mathbb R,\ y\in\{0,1\}.
$$
This guarantees $\mathbb P(X\le t\mid Y=y)=\mathbb P(X<t\mid Y=y)$ exactly, for every threshold and class. For the upper-tail rule $\hat Y_t=\mathbb 1\{X\ge t\}$, write
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{TPR}^+(t)
& :=\mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=1),\\
\mathrm{FPR}^+(t)
& :=\mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=0).
\end{align*}
$$

#### Threshold reversal

Keeping the class labels unchanged and reversing the rule to $\hat Y_t^\star=\mathbb 1\{X<t\}$ sends the operating point as
$$
\boxed{
(\mathrm{FPR}^+(t),\mathrm{TPR}^+(t)) \longmapsto (1-\mathrm{FPR}^+(t),\,1-\mathrm{TPR}^+(t)).
}
$$

:::: {#thm-roc-threshold-reversal}

# Central symmetry

The ROC curve under threshold reversal (class labels fixed) is the central reflection of the original ROC curve about $(0.5,0.5)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-threshold-reversal')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-threshold-reversal .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-threshold-reversal .proof-content}
Under the reversed rule $\hat Y_t^\star=\mathbb 1\{X<t\}$,
$$
\mathbb P(X<t\mid Y=0) = 1-\mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=0) = 1-\mathrm{FPR}^+(t), \qquad \mathbb P(X<t\mid Y=1) = 1-\mathrm{TPR}^+(t).
$$
Thus $(\mathrm{FPR}^+(t),\mathrm{TPR}^+(t))\mapsto(1-\mathrm{FPR}^+(t),\,1-\mathrm{TPR}^+(t))$, a central reflection about $(0.5,0.5)$.
:::
::::

##### Class label swap

Keeping the rule unchanged but swapping the labels, $Y^\star=1-Y$, $\hat Y_t^\star=\mathbb 1\{X\ge t\}$, sends the operating point as
$$
\boxed{
(\mathrm{FPR}^+(t),\mathrm{TPR}^+(t)) \longmapsto (\mathrm{TPR}^+(t),\,\mathrm{FPR}^+(t)).
}
$$

:::: {#thm-roc-class-swap}

# Main-diagonal symmetry

Under class-label swapping with the rule unchanged, the ROC curve is the reflection of the original curve about the main diagonal $y=x$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-class-swap')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-class-swap .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-class-swap .proof-content}
Since $Y^\star=1-Y$, $\{Y^\star=0\}=\{Y=1\}$ and $\{Y^\star=1\}=\{Y=0\}$. Under the unchanged rule,
$$
\mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y^\star=0) = \mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=1) = \mathrm{TPR}^+(t), \qquad \mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y^\star=1) = \mathrm{FPR}^+(t).
$$
Thus $(\mathrm{FPR}^+(t),\mathrm{TPR}^+(t))\mapsto(\mathrm{TPR}^+(t),\,\mathrm{FPR}^+(t))$, a reflection about $y=x$.
:::
::::

##### Class label swap with threshold reversal

Swapping the labels **and** reversing the rule, $Y^\star=1-Y$, $\hat Y_t^\star=\mathbb 1\{X\le t\}$, sends the operating point as
$$
\boxed{
(\mathrm{FPR}^+(t),\mathrm{TPR}^+(t)) \longmapsto (1-\mathrm{TPR}^+(t),\,1-\mathrm{FPR}^+(t)).
}
$$

:::: {#thm-roc-class-inversion}

# Anti-diagonal symmetry

Under simultaneous class-label swapping and threshold reversal, the ROC curve is the reflection of the original curve about the anti-diagonal $y=1-x$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-class-inversion')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-class-inversion .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-class-inversion .proof-content}
As above, $\{Y^\star=0\}=\{Y=1\}$, $\{Y^\star=1\}=\{Y=0\}$. Under the reversed rule $\hat Y_t^\star=\mathbb 1\{X\le t\}$, atomlessness gives $\mathbb P(X\le t\mid Y=y)=\mathbb P(X<t\mid Y=y)$, and $\{X<t\}=\{X\ge t\}^c$ gives
$$
\mathbb P(X\le t\mid Y^\star=0) = \mathbb P(X<t\mid Y=1) = 1-\mathrm{TPR}^+(t), \qquad \mathbb P(X\le t\mid Y^\star=1) = 1-\mathrm{FPR}^+(t).
$$
Thus $(\mathrm{FPR}^+(t),\mathrm{TPR}^+(t))\mapsto(1-\mathrm{TPR}^+(t),\,1-\mathrm{FPR}^+(t))$, a reflection about $y=1-x$.
:::
::::

##### Summary and visualization

::: {style="font-size:90%; margin: 1em 0;"}
| Transformation | FPR$'$ | TPR$'$ | Geometric interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Threshold reversal: $X<t \leftrightarrow X\ge t$ | $1-\mathrm{FPR}$ | $1-\mathrm{TPR}$ | Central symmetry about $(0.5,0.5)$ |
| Class label swap: $Y=0\leftrightarrow Y=1$ | $\mathrm{TPR}$ | $\mathrm{FPR}$ | Reflection across the main diagonal |
| Both (reverse rule + swap labels) | $1-\mathrm{TPR}$ | $1-\mathrm{FPR}$ | Reflection across the anti-diagonal $y=1-x$ |

: Simple transformations of the ROC operating point {#tbl-roc-transformations .striped .hover}
:::

These three transformations, together with the identity, preserve the curve's overall shape. As noted above, none of them depends on the class prevalence $\pi_1=\mathbb P(Y=1)$.
You can verify this directly with the interactive below

Use the **Threshold ($\pi$)** slider to move along the ROC curve and watch the operating point change; the **Prevalence** slider confirms that the ROC curve itself is unaffected by class imbalance, however that slider is moved. The plot also shows the reversed-rule and class-inverted curves described above.

## ROC curve for common distributions



Below we summarize the ROC curves for classic location-scale distributions, along with the exponential case.
Throughout, we assume that $Z_0, Z_1$ are independent and identically distributed with a common continuous CDF $F$.
We define the location-scale variables as:

$$
\begin{align*}
X_0 & = \sigma_0 Z_0 + \mu_0,\\
X_1 & = \sigma_1 Z_1 + \mu_1,
\end{align*}
$$
where $\sigma_0 > 0$ and $\sigma_1 > 0$ are the scale parameters, and $\mu_0, \mu_1 \in \mathbb{R}$ are the location parameters. We use the following notation:

- $\Delta = (\mu_1 - \mu_0) / \sigma_1$ (standardized separation)
- $\rho = \sigma_0 / \sigma_1 > 0$ (scale ratio)
- $\Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^z \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-u^2/2} \, du$ (standard Gaussian CDF)
- $[x]_0^1 = \max(0, \min(1, x))$ (clipping function)
- $(x)_+= \max(0,x)$


::: {style="font-size:90%; margin: 1em 0;"}
   Law of $Z$ | CDF $F(z)$ | $\mathrm{TPR}(\mathrm{FPR})$ | Symmetric |
 |------------|-------------|------------------------|:---------:|
 | **Gaussian** | $\Phi(z)$ | $\Phi\bigl(\Delta + \rho \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})\bigr)$ | ✓ |
 |**Cauchy** | $\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{\tan^{-1}z}{\pi}$ | $\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{\tan^{-1}(\Delta + \rho\, \tan(\pi(\mathrm{FPR} - \tfrac{1}{2})\bigr)\bigr)}{\pi}$ | ✓ |
 | **Logistic** | $\dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$ | $\dfrac{e^{\Delta} \mathrm{FPR}^{\rho}}{e^{\Delta} \mathrm{FPR}^{\rho} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR})^{\rho}}$ | ✓ |
 | **Uniform** $(-\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})$ | $\bigl[z + \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl]_0^1$ | $\bigl[\Delta + \tfrac{1 - \rho}{2} + \rho \mathrm{FPR}\bigl]_0^1$ | ✓ |
 | **Gumbel** | $\exp\bigl(-e^{-z}\bigr)$ | $1 - \tfrac{1}{\exp\Bigl(e^{\Delta} \bigl(-\ln(1 - \mathrm{FPR})\bigr)^\rho \Bigr)}$ | ✗ |
 | **Exp.** | $(1 - e^{-z})_+$ | $\min\bigl(e^{\Delta} \mathrm{FPR}^{\rho}, 1\bigr)$ | ✗ |

: ROC curves for common distributions {#tbl-distributions .striped .hover}
:::



**Where the table comes from.** All the rows follow from a single identity (@thm-location-scale-roc): for $X_y=\sigma_yZ_y+\mu_y$ with $Z_0,Z_1$ i.i.d. with CDF $F$,
$$
\mathrm{TPR}=1-F\bigl(\rho\,F^{-1}(1-\mathrm{FPR})-\Delta\bigr),
$$
which simplifies to $\mathrm{TPR}=F\bigl(\Delta+\rho\,F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})\bigr)$ when $F$ is symmetric (@cor-symmetric-roc). The statements, the proofs, and the row-by-row computations (Gaussian, Cauchy, Logistic, Uniform, Gumbel, Exponential) are collected in [Appendix A](#sec-app-roc).

**Visualization**

The horizontal black line marks the current threshold $t$; the darker-shaded region of each density is $\{X\le t\}$ (the portion of that class predicted *negative* under the rule $\hat Y_t=\mathbb 1\{X\ge t\}$) while the lighter region above the line is predicted *positive*.

The title above the plot reports the current $\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$, $\rho = \sigma_0/\sigma_1$.

**ROC curve for classic distributions**

:::

[Note]{.underline}: Visually, the TPR is the ratio of the light blue area over the full blue area on the left, while the FPR is the ratio of the light red area over the full red area (right).

**Interpretation**

$\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$ measures the (scale-standardized) separation between $X_0$ and $X_1$; $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1$ compares their spread. Together they set the difficulty and shape of the ROC curve.

* **$\rho=1$:** the usual equal-scale model, $\mathrm{TPR}=F(\Delta+F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}))$ for symmetric $F$ — e.g. the binormal case $\mathrm{TPR}=\Phi(\Delta+\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}))$.
* **$\Delta=0,\ \rho=1$:** $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$, and the ROC curve is the diagonal (random guessing). Note $\Delta=0$ alone is *not* enough when $\rho\ne1$: equal location with unequal scale still separates the classes, via spread rather than location.
* **$\rho\ne1$:** the curve need not be symmetric about the anti-diagonal or concave everywhere — if $\rho<1$ (sick population more dispersed), the curve can dip toward the diagonal near one corner before rising, a non-concave S-shape sometimes seen in real assay data.
* **$\Delta\to\infty$** (fixed $\rho$): the classes separate perfectly, and the curve approaches the ideal curve through $(0,1)$.


Now we illustrate the empirical counterpart, when one samples elements from the distributions but without access to the true densities.

```{python}
#| echo: false

def roc(thresholds, y_true, score):
    # Extracted from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/25009284/how-to-plot-roc-curve-in-python
    fpr = []  # false positive rate
    tpr = []  # true positive rate

    # get number of positive and negative examples in the dataset
    P = sum(y_true)
    N = len(y_true) - P

    # iterate through all thresholds and determine fraction of true positives
    # and false positives found at this threshold
    for thresh in thresholds:
        FP = 0
        TP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] >= thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        fpr.append(FP / float(N))
        tpr.append(TP / float(P))
    return tpr, fpr
```

**Note**: the jittering on the x-axis for the scatter plots is not meaningful but only here for visualization.


### Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)

The **Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)** is a scalar summary of the classifier’s discriminative power across all thresholds.
Because the ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate for every possible decision boundary, its area ​quantifies the probability that a randomly chosen positive instance is ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative instance.
Often the AUC is used to measure overall performance: the larger the AUC, the better the assay discriminates between the two classes.


:::: {#thm-randomized-roc}

# Randomized ROC curve

Let $X_0$ and $X_1$ be independent, distributed as the conditional laws of $X$ given $Y=0$ and $Y=1$, respectively:
$$
X_0 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=0), \qquad X_1 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=1).
$$
As conditional laws of a real random variable $X$, both $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite.

For $s\in[0,1]$, define
$$
t(s) := \sup\{t\in\mathbb R : \mathbb P(X_0\ge t)\ge s\} \ \in\ \mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\},
$$
and
$$
\lambda(s) :=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s-\mathbb P(X_0>t(s))}{\mathbb P(X_0=t(s))}, & \mathbb P(X_0=t(s))>0,\\[6pt]
0, & \mathbb P(X_0=t(s))=0.
\end{cases}
$$

Define the randomized decision rule
$$
\phi_s(x) = \mathbf 1\{x>t(s)\} + \lambda(s)\mathbf 1\{x=t(s)\}.
$$

Then $\lambda(s)\in[0,1]$ is well defined for every $s\in[0,1]$, and
$$
\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s) := \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_0)] = s,
$$
so the (randomized) ROC curve $\operatorname{ROC}(s):=\operatorname{TPR}(\phi_s)=\mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)]$, $s\in[0,1]$, is well defined for any laws of $X_0$ and $X_1$.

Moreover, at every atom $c$ of $X_0$ (i.e., $\mathbb P(X_0=c)>0$), $\operatorname{ROC}$ is affine on the interval $\bigl(\mathbb P(X_0>c),\ \mathbb P(X_0\ge c)\bigr]$, of length $p_c$, with slope $\mathbb P(X_1=c)/P(X_0=c)$.

Finally,
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{AUC} := \int_0^1\operatorname{ROC}(s)\,ds = \mathbb P(X_1>X_0) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_1=X_0).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-randomized-roc')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-randomized-roc .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-randomized-roc .proof-content}
Throughout, write $G_0(t):=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$ for the survival function of $X_0$, and $G_0(x+):=\lim_{u\downarrow x}G_0(u)$ for its right limit at any $x\in\mathbb R$. As a survival function, $G_0$ is non-increasing, and it is left-continuous, $G_0(x)=\lim_{u\uparrow x}G_0(u)$, since $\{X_0\ge u_n\}\downarrow\{X_0\ge x\}$ along any $u_n\uparrow x$; likewise $\{X_0\ge u_n\}\uparrow\{X_0>x\}$ along any $u_n\downarrow x$ gives $G_0(x+)=\mathbb P(X_0>x)$, so
$$
P(X_0=x):=G_0(x)-G_0(x+)=\mathbb P(X_0=x)
$$
is exactly the atomic mass of $X_0$ at $x$. Since $X_0$ is a.s. finite, continuity of measure applied to the nested events $\{X_0\ge t\}$ as $t\to\mp\infty$ also gives
$$
\lim_{t\to-\infty}G_0(t)=1, \qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}G_0(t)=0.
$$

**Step 1 (existence of $t(s)$).** Call $L\subseteq\mathbb R$ a *lower set* if $t\in L,\,u\le t\Rightarrow u\in L$. Fix $s\in(0,1)$ and set $A_s:=\{t:G_0(t)\ge s\}$. Since $G_0$ is non-increasing, $A_s$ is a lower set; since $G_0\to1>s$ as $t\to-\infty$ and $G_0\to0<s$ as $t\to\infty$, $A_s$ is nonempty and bounded above, so
$$
t(s):=\sup A_s\ \in\ \mathbb R
$$
is well defined. In fact $A_s=(-\infty,t(s)]$: any $t<t(s)$ is not an upper bound of $A_s$, hence lies in $A_s$ by the lower-set property; and $t(s)\in A_s$ by left-continuity of $G_0$ along $t_n\uparrow t(s)$, $t_n\in A_s$.

For the endpoints $s\in\{0,1\}$, the same set $A_s=\{t:G_0(t)\ge s\}$ is used, with the convention $\sup\emptyset=-\infty$: since $G_0\le1$ everywhere, $A_0=\mathbb R$ and $t(0)=+\infty$; and $A_1=\{t:G_0(t)=1\}$, which is a (possibly empty) lower set, giving $t(1)\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$ with $A_1=(-\infty,t(1)]$ by the same argument (or $A_1=\emptyset$, $t(1)=-\infty$, if $G_0(t)<1$ for every $t$).

**Step 2 (level sets, and the defining inequality).** For $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$
t(s)=x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_0(x+) < s \le G_0(x). \tag{$\dagger$}
$$

*Proof.* By Step 1, $t(s)=x$ iff $x\in A_s$ and no $y>x$ lies in $A_s$, i.e.,
$$
G_0(x)\ge s \qquad\text{and}\qquad G_0(y)<s\ \ \forall y>x.
$$
Since $G_0$ is non-increasing, $\sup_{y>x}G_0(y)=G_0(x+)$, so the second condition is equivalent to $s>G_0(x+)$; this proves $(\dagger)$.

Taking $x=t(s)$ in $(\dagger)$ yields both the defining inequality and the atom size at the threshold:
$$
\begin{cases}
G_0(t(s)+) \ \le\ s\ \le\ G_0(t(s)), \\
G_0(t(s))-G_0(t(s)+) = \mathbb P(X_0=t(s)). \tag{$\ast$}
\end{cases}
$$


**Step 3 ($\phi_s$ attains $\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s)=s$ exactly).** By $(\ast)$,
$$
0\ \le\ s-G_0(t(s)+)\ \le\ P(X_0=t(s)),
$$
so whenever $P(X_0=t(s))>0$, $\lambda(s)=\dfrac{s-G_0(t(s)+)}{P(X_0=t(s))}\in[0,1]$ . If instead $P(X_0=t(s))=0$, the two bounds coincide and force $s=G_0(t(s)+)$; the definition sets $\lambda(s):=0$ in this case, and its value has no impact since it multiplies the null event $\{X_0=t(s)\}$. In either case,
$$
\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s) = \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_0)] = G_0(t(s)+) + \lambda(s)\,P(X_0=t(s)) = s.
$$


**Step 4 (affine property of ROC).** Fix $c$ with $P(X_0=c)>0$, and let $s\in(G_0(c+),G_0(c)]$. By $(\dagger)$, $t(s)=c$ throughout this interval, so substituting $t(s)=c$ into the definition of $\lambda$, legitimate since $P(X_0=t(s))=P(X_0=c)>0$ there, gives
$$
\lambda(s) = \frac{s-G_0(c+)}{P(X_0=c)},
$$
a linear, increasing function of $s$, running from $0$ at $s=G_0(c+)$ to $1$ at $s=G_0(c)$. Hence
$\operatorname{ROC}(s) = \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)] = \mathbb P(X_1>c) + \lambda(s)\,\mathbb P(X_1=c)$
is affine in $s$ on $(G_0(c+),G_0(c)]$, an interval of length $P(X_0=c)$, with slope $\mathbb P(X_1=c)/P(X_0=c)$.

**Step 5 (AUC).** Since $t(\cdot)$ is non-increasing (its sublevel sets $A_s$ are nested in $s$, by Step 1) and $\lambda(\cdot)$ is Borel where defined, $(s,x)\mapsto\phi_s(x)$ is jointly measurable, $[0,1]$-valued, so Tonelli's theorem gives
$$
\operatorname{AUC} = \int_0^1 \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)]\,ds = \mathbb E\!\left[\int_0^1 \phi_s(X_1)\,ds\right].
$$

Fix $x\in\mathbb R$. By $(\dagger)$, up to the single (Lebesgue-null) point $G(x+)$, the interval $[0,1]$ splits into three sets, according to the position of $t(s)$ relative to $x$:
$$
\begin{align*}
\{s:t(s)>x\} &= [0,G(x+)], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)>x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0>x), \\
\{s:t(s)=x\} &= (G(x+),G(x)], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)=x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0=x), \\
\{s:t(s)<x\} &= (G(x),1], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)<x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0<x).
\end{align*}
$$

On each of these three sets, $\phi_s(x)=\mathbf 1\{x>t(s)\}+\lambda(s)\mathbf 1\{x=t(s)\}$ takes a simple form:
$$
\phi_s(x) =
\begin{cases}
0, & t(s)>x,\\
\lambda(s), & t(s)=x,\\
1, & t(s)<x.
\end{cases}
$$
Hence $\int_0^1\phi_s(x)\,ds$ splits into three integrals, one over each set:
$$
\int_0^1\phi_s(x)\,ds
= \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)>x\}} 0\,ds}_{=\,0}
\ +\ \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)=x\}} \lambda(s)\,ds}_{=:I(x)}
\ +\ \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)<x\}} 1\,ds}_{=\,\mathbb P(X_0<x)}.
$$

It remains to compute $I(x)=\int_{(G(x+),G(x)]} \lambda(s)\,ds$, by splitting on whether $x$ is an atom of $X_0$:

- If $P(X_0=x)=0$: the domain of integration is Lebesgue-null, so $I(x)=0=\tfrac12\,P(X_0=x)$.
- If $P(X_0=x)>0$: by Step 4 (with $c=x$), $\lambda(s)$ runs linearly from $0$ to $1$ as $s$ ranges over $(G(x+),G(x)]$. The average of a function running linearly between $0$ and $1$ over an interval is $\tfrac12$ (the midpoint of its range), so $I(x)=P(X_0=x)\cdot\tfrac12$.

Either way, $I(x)=\tfrac12\,P(X_0=x)$, and therefore
$$
\int_0^1 \phi_s(x)\,ds = \mathbb P(X_0<x) + \tfrac12\,P(X_0=x) = \mathbb P(X_0<x) + \tfrac12\,\mathbb P(X_0=x).
$$

Substituting $x=X_1$, taking expectations, and using the tower property,
$$
\operatorname{AUC} = \mathbb P(X_0<X_1) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_0=X_1) = \mathbb P(X_1>X_0) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_1=X_0).
$$

:::

::::


For continuous random variables (with no point masses), the AUC reduces to the probability that $X_1 > X_0$.


:::: {#cor-continuous-auc}


# AUC for continuous distributions

Let $X_0 \sim \mathcal{L}(X \mid Y=0)$ and $X_1 \sim \mathcal{L}(X \mid Y=1)$ be independent continuous random variables (no point masses).

Then, the AUC of the ROC curve simplifies to:

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{AUC} = \mathbb{P}(X_1 > X_0).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('cor-continuous-auc')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-cor-continuous-auc .proof-arrow} **Proof**
:::

::: {#proof-content-cor-continuous-auc .proof-content}

Since $X_0$ and $X_1$ are continuous, $\mathbb{P}(X_1 = X_0) = 0$. By the randomized ROC theorem (@thm-randomized-roc), the AUC is:

$$
\operatorname{AUC} = \mathbb{P}(X_1 > X_0) + \tfrac12 \mathbb{P}(X_1 = X_0) = \mathbb{P}(X_1 > X_0).
$$

:::
::::

AUC is the probability that a randomly selected positive case receives a higher score than a randomly selected negative case, with ties counted as half a win.

<!-- This probabilistic reading of the AUC (the chance that a randomly drawn positive case outscores a randomly drawn negative case) is not just a theoretical curiosity: it is directly *estimable* from data, since it is itself a probability that can be approximated by counting concordant pairs in a finite sample. -->

Replacing $X_0,X_1$ by two independent samples and $\mathbb P(X_1>X_0)$ by the corresponding sample proportion gives exactly the classical **Mann-Whitney $U$ statistic** from nonparametric statistics, providing the empirical, plug-in counterpart to @cor-continuous-auc.




:::: {#thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney}

# Empirical AUC and Mann-Whitney U Statistic

Let $X_{1,1}, \ldots, X_{1,n_1}$ be an i.i.d. sample from $X_1 \sim \mathcal{L}(X \mid Y=1)$ and $X_{0,1}, \ldots, X_{0,n_0}$ be an i.i.d. sample from $X_0 \sim \mathcal{L}(X \mid Y=0)$, with both samples independent of each other. Assume $X_1$ and $X_0$ are continuous random variables (no point masses).

Let $R_1$ be the sum of the ranks of the $X_{1,i}$ values in the combined sample of size $n_1 + n_0$ (ranks assigned in ascending order, so the smallest value has rank $1$). The **Mann-Whitney U statistic** for the positive group is defined as:
$$
U_1 = R_1 - \frac{n_1 (n_1 + 1)}{2}= \sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}).
$$

Then, the **empirical AUC** of the ROC curve is equivalent to the normalized Mann-Whitney U statistic:
$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\operatorname{AUC}} = \frac{1}{n_1 n_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney .proof-arrow} **Proof**
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney .proof-content}

1. **Rank Sum Interpretation**:
   The term $R_1$ in $U_1$ is the sum of the ranks of the $X_{1,i}$ values in the combined sample of size $n_1 + n_0$. For continuous distributions, all $X_{1,i}$ and $X_{0,j}$ are distinct almost surely, so the rank of each $X_{1,i}$ equals the number of $X_{0,j}$ values it exceeds, plus the number of $X_{1,i'}$ values ($i' \neq i$) it exceeds, plus $1$ (for its own position):
   $$
   R_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} \left( \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}) + \sum_{i' \neq i} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{1,i'}) + 1 \right).
   $$

2. **Simplification of $R_1$**:
   The double sum over $i' \neq i$ counts, for each unordered pair $\{i,i'\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n_1\}$, the (exactly one) index of the pair whose value is larger : so it counts each of the $\binom{n_1}{2}=\frac{n_1(n_1-1)}{2}$ pairs exactly once. Writing
   $$
   S := \sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j})
   $$
   for the number of cross-sample pairs where the positive-group value is larger, this gives
   $$
   R_1 = S + \frac{n_1(n_1-1)}{2} + n_1 = S + \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2},
   $$
   using $\frac{n_1(n_1-1)}{2}+n_1=\frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2}$.

3. **Link to $U_1$**:
   Substituting the expression for $R_1$ from Step 2 directly into the definition of $U_1$,
   $$
   U_1 = R_1 - \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2} = \left(S + \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2}\right) - \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2} = S,
   $$
   so $U_1$ is exactly the count of cross-sample pairs with $X_{1,i}>X_{0,j}$:
   $$
   U_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}).
   $$
4. **Empirical AUC**:
   Recall that $\widehat{\operatorname{AUC}}$ is defined as the fraction of positive/negative pairs correctly ordered by the score, i.e.
   $$
   \widehat{\operatorname{AUC}} = \frac{1}{n_1 n_0} \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}) = \frac{S}{n_1n_0}.
   $$
   By Step 3, $S=U_1$, so
   $$
   \widehat{\operatorname{AUC}} = \frac{U_1}{n_1 n_0}.
   $$

:::
::::



Class label swap, threshold reversal or both (reverse rule + swap labels) preserve the ROC curve's overall shape.

A natural next question is how these geometric symmetries affect the curve's AUC.
The following theorem works out exactly what happens in each case.



:::: {#thm-auc-class-inversion}

# AUC under threshold reversal and class inversion

Assume $X\mid Y=0$ and $X\mid Y=1$ are atomless and almost surely finite. Write $\operatorname{AUC}^\star$ for the AUC of the transformed problem in each case below. Then:

- under threshold reversal alone, $\boxed{\operatorname{AUC}^\star = 1-\operatorname{AUC}}$;
- under class label swap alone, $\boxed{\operatorname{AUC}^\star = 1-\operatorname{AUC}}$;
- under both together (the anti-diagonal transform), $\boxed{\operatorname{AUC}^\star = \operatorname{AUC}}$, leaving the AUC unchanged.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-auc-class-inversion')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-auc-class-inversion .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-auc-class-inversion .proof-content}

Write $u:=\mathrm{FPR}^+(t)$, $f(u):=\mathrm{TPR}^+(t)$, so $\operatorname{AUC}=\int_0^1 f(u)\,du$, with $f$ non-decreasing (@thm-roc-monotonicity), $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$ (@lem-roc-endpoints). Let $R:=\{(x,y):0\le x\le1,\,0\le y\le f(x)\}$, of area $\operatorname{AUC}$.

**Threshold reversal.** The transformed curve is $g(x'):=1-f(1-x')$. Reflecting $R$ through $(0.5,0.5)$ sends $(x,y)\mapsto(1-x,1-y)$, and $0\le y\le f(x)$ becomes $1-f(1-x')\le y'\le1$, the region **above** $g$, of area $1-\operatorname{AUC}^\star$. Since central reflection preserves area, $1-\operatorname{AUC}^\star=\operatorname{AUC}$, *i.e.*, $\operatorname{AUC}^\star=1-\operatorname{AUC}$.

**Class label swap.** The transformed curve is $g:=f^{-1}$ (generalized inverse). Reflecting $R$ across $y=x$ sends $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, and $0\le x\le f(y)$ becomes, by monotonicity of $f$, $y\ge f^{-1}(x)=g(x)$, the same region above $g$, of area $1-\operatorname{AUC}^\star$. Reflection across a line preserves area, so once more $\operatorname{AUC}^\star=1-\operatorname{AUC}$.

**Both together.** The two transforms commute at the level of the operating point, so applying one after the other composes the two identities just derived: $\operatorname{AUC}\mapsto1-\operatorname{AUC}\mapsto1-(1-\operatorname{AUC})=\operatorname{AUC}$.

:::
::::

**Interpretation.** Only the composite (anti-diagonal) transform preserves AUC exactly; the two individual transforms each send $A\mapsto1-A$. This is intuitive: reversing the rule alone, or swapping the labels alone, each turns a good classifier into a bad one for the *new* problem (a classifier that correctly separates $X_0$ from $X_1$ under the original labeling is simply mislabeling everything once only one of the two conventions is flipped). On the other hand, flipping *both* conventions together restores consistency, since relabeling "positive" to mean "low score" and simultaneously testing for "low score" recovers a description of the exact same underlying discrimination ability. The fixed point of $A\mapsto1-A$ at $A=\tfrac12$ (random guessing) is the one case where all three transforms leave AUC unchanged, since $1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$.

You can verify this directly with the interactive above, see @fig-gaussian-symmetric-roc: the "ROC curve" and "Class swap + threshold rev." curves in the plot share the same AUC, while "Threshold reversal" and "Class label swap" alone each trace out the complementary area.


## The Precision–Recall curve

The **precision–recall (PR) curve** describes the trade-off between recall and precision as the decision threshold $t$ varies. It is the parametric curve

$$
\left\{
\bigl(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\bigr)
: t\in\mathbb{R}
\right\},
$$

where recall is the true-positive rate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Recall}(t)
&=\mathrm{TPR}(t)\\
&=\mathbb{P}(X\geq t\mid Y=1)\\
&=\mathbb{P}(X_1\geq t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Precision, in contrast, is the probability that an individual truly belongs to the positive class, given that the test predicts a positive result:

$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid X\geq t).
$$

Unlike recall and the false-positive rate, which are conditional on the true class, precision also depends on the **prevalence** of the positive class in the population of interest. We denote the class prevalences by

$$
\pi_1=\mathbb{P}(Y=1),
\qquad
\pi_0=\mathbb{P}(Y=0)=1-\pi_1.
$$

### Empirical estimation

Given a sample $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, let

$$
n_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}\{Y_i=1\},
\qquad
n_0=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}\{Y_i=0\}
$$

denote the numbers of positive and negative observations, respectively. At a threshold $t$, the numbers of true positives and false positives are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{TP}(t)
&=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\mathbb{1}\{Y_i=1,\ X_i\geq t\},\\
\mathrm{FP}(t)
&=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\mathbb{1}\{Y_i=0,\ X_i\geq t\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The empirical recall and precision are then

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\mathrm{Recall}}(t)
&=\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{n_1},\\[6pt]
\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(t)
&=\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}
{\mathrm{TP}(t)+\mathrm{FP}(t)}.
\end{aligned}
}
$$

Empirical recall measures the fraction of positive observations detected by the test, while empirical precision measures the fraction of predicted-positive observations that are truly positive.

If no observations are predicted positive, then $\mathrm{TP}(t)+\mathrm{FP}(t)=0$ and empirical precision is undefined. Implementations of PR curves may adopt a convention for this endpoint, which should be considered when comparing empirical curves.

### Precision in terms of TPR, FPR, and prevalence

The following theorem makes explicit how prevalence enters the precision formula.

:::: {#thm-precision-formula}

# Precision in terms of TPR, FPR, and prevalence

Let $\pi_1=\mathbb{P}(Y=1)$ and $\pi_0=\mathbb{P}(Y=0)$. For every threshold $t$ such that $\mathbb{P}(X\geq t)>0$,

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(t)
=
\frac{
\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)
}{
\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)
+
\pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)
}.
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-precision-formula')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-precision-formula .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-precision-formula .proof-content}

By the law of total probability,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X\geq t)
&=
\mathbb{P}(X\geq t\mid Y=1)\pi_1\\
&\quad+
\mathbb{P}(X\geq t\mid Y=0)\pi_0\\
&=
\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)
+
\pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Furthermore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Y=1,\ X\geq t)
&=
\mathbb{P}(X\geq t\mid Y=1)\pi_1\\
&=
\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

By the definition of conditional probability,

$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=1,\ X\geq t)}
{\mathbb{P}(X\geq t)}.
$$

Substituting the expressions above yields the claimed formula.

:::
::::

### Consequences

**Dependence on prevalence.** For fixed class-conditional score distributions, both $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ remain unchanged when prevalence changes. The ROC curve therefore remains unchanged, whereas the PR curve generally changes through the prevalence terms $\pi_1$ and $\pi_0$ in the theorem. In particular, when positive cases become less common, precision typically decreases at a fixed threshold. This is why precision values should be compared cautiously across studies with different prevalences.

**The positive fraction in our dataset.** In our COVID-19 example, the benchmark contains 976 pre-pandemic negative samples and 536 confirmed positive samples. The positive fraction is therefore

$$
\frac{536}{976+536}\approx 35.45\%.
$$

This fraction describes the **composition of the benchmark dataset**, not necessarily the prevalence of COVID-19 in a clinical population. If the benchmark's class composition differs from that of the target population, its empirical PR curve and average precision may not represent the predictive performance expected in that population. The ROC curve and AUC, by contrast, are unaffected by prevalence when the class-conditional score distributions are held fixed.

**The PR baseline under random guessing.** As $t\to-\infty$, the classifier predicts every individual positive. Under the usual endpoint limits, $\mathrm{TPR}(t)\to1$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\to1$; consequently,

$$
\mathrm{Recall}(t)\to1,
\qquad
\mathrm{Precision}(t)\to\pi_1.
$$

Thus, the all-positive endpoint of the PR curve is $(1,\pi_1)$.

More generally, under random guessing, the class-conditional score distributions coincide, so

$$
\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathrm{FPR}(t)
$$

for every threshold $t$ (see @thm-random-guessing). The theorem then gives

$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\pi_1
$$

whenever the denominator is positive. The **random-guessing baseline is therefore a horizontal line at precision $\pi_1$**, unlike the diagonal ROC baseline, which does not depend on prevalence.



One mathematical nuance worth preserving: the final statement assumes the threshold selects a nonzero fraction of the population. At extreme thresholds where $\mathbb{P}(X\geq t)=0$, precision is undefined, rather than equal to prevalence. Also, the random-guessing result is a population-level statement; empirical PR curves can fluctuate around the prevalence baseline in finite samples.


The Python code to compute this curve is provided below.
```{python}
def precision_recall(thresholds, y_true, score):
    precision = []
    recall = []

    P = sum(y_true)

    for thresh in thresholds:
        FP = 0
        TP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] > thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        recall.append(TP / float(P))
        precision.append(TP / float(TP + FP) if (TP + FP) > 0 else 1.0)
    return precision, recall
```


### Properties

#### Endpoints

Throughout, $\pi_1\in(0,1)$, $\pi_0=1-\pi_1$, and $X_0,X_1$ are almost surely finite. For the threshold rule $\hat Y_t(X)=\mathbb 1\{X\ge t\}$,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Recall}(t) & =\mathbb P(X_1\ge t),\\
\mathrm{Precision}(t) &=\frac{\pi_1\,\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)}{\pi_1\,\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)+\pi_0\,\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)},
\end{align*}
$$
where $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\mathbb P(Y=1\mid\hat Y_t=1)$ is defined whenever the denominator is positive.

:::: {#lem-pr-endpoint}

# Universal endpoint of the PR curve

There exists $t_0\in\mathbb R$ such that the denominator of $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ is positive for all $t\le t_0$, and
$$
\boxed{\lim_{t\to-\infty}\bigl(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\bigr)=(1,\pi_1).}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-pr-endpoint')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-pr-endpoint .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-pr-endpoint .proof-content}

Since $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite, the events $\{X_y\ge t\}$ increase to $\{X_y>-\infty\}$, which has probability $1$, as $t\downarrow-\infty$. By continuity of probability measures,
$$
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\mathbb P(X_y\ge t)=1,\qquad y\in\{0,1\}.
$$
Hence $\mathrm{Recall}(t)\to1$, and the denominator of $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ tends to $\pi_1+\pi_0=1$. In particular it is positive for all $t$ sufficiently negative, so $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ is defined there. Since the limit of the denominator is $1\neq0$, the quotient rule for limits gives
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)\longrightarrow\frac{\pi_1\cdot1}{\pi_1\cdot1+\pi_0\cdot1}=\pi_1.
$$

:::
::::


**Remark (the other end, $\mathrm{Recall}\to0$).** The limit as $t\to+\infty$ is *not* universal: numerator and denominator of $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ both tend to $0$, and
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\Bigl(1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\,\frac{\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)}{\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)}\Bigr)^{-1}
$$
is governed by the tail ratio $\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)/\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$. For instance:

- $X_y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_y,\sigma^2)$ with $\mu_1>\mu_0$: the ratio tends to $0$, and the curve ends at $(0,1)$.
- $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$: the ratio is $\equiv1$, and the curve ends at $(0,\pi_1)$.
- $X_y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_y,\sigma^2)$ with $\mu_1<\mu_0$: the ratio tends to $+\infty$, and the curve ends at $(0,0)$.



### Extreme Cases


#### Perfect Classifier

:::: {#thm-perfect-pr-separation}

# PR curve for a perfect classifier

Suppose there exists a threshold $t^\star \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for $\hat{Y}_t = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t^\star) = 0, \qquad \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t^\star) = 1.
$$
Then,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Recall}(t^\star) = 1, \qquad \mathrm{Precision}(t^\star) = 1,}
$$
Moreover, $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\equiv1$ for **every** $t\ge t^\star$: the PR curve is flat at $\mathrm{Precision}=1$ across the whole range $\mathrm{Recall}\in[0,1]$, and only drops vertically at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$, to the (universal) endpoint $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$ as $t\to-\infty$. In particular the curve passes through $(1,1)$, $(0,1)$, and $(1,\pi_1)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-perfect-pr-separation')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-perfect-pr-separation .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-perfect-pr-separation .proof-content}
**The point at $t^\star$.** By definition,
$$
\mathrm{Recall}(t^\star) = 
\mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t^\star) = 1, \quad 
\mathrm{Precision}(t^\star) = 
\frac{\pi_1 \cdot 1}{\pi_1 \cdot 1 + \pi_0 \cdot 0} = 1.
$$

**The flat segment.** By @thm-roc-monotonicity, $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$ is non-increasing in $t$. Since $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star)=0$ and $\mathrm{FPR}\ge0$ always, monotonicity gives $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\le\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star)=0$ for every $t\ge t^\star$, so
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t) = 0 \qquad\text{for all } t\ge t^\star.
$$
Consequently, for any $t\ge t^\star$ with $\mathrm{TPR}(t)>0$,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + \pi_0\cdot0} = 1.
$$
In the case that $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=0$, $\mathrm{Precision}(t):=1$ by the standing convention. Either way, $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\equiv1$ for every $t\ge t^\star$. 


**The endpoints.** As $t$ ranges over $[t^\star,\infty)$, $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ decreases from $1$ (at $t^\star$) to $0$ (as $t\to\infty$, by @lem-roc-endpoints), tracing the flat segment $\{(\mathrm{Recall},1):\mathrm{Recall}\in[0,1]\}$. As $t\to-\infty$, $\mathrm{TPR}(t)\to1$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\to1$ (again @lem-roc-endpoints), giving $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\to\dfrac{\pi_1}{\pi_1+\pi_0}=\pi_1$: the universal endpoint $(1,\pi_1)$ (this holds for *any* model, see @thm-precision-formula).
:::

::::


#### Always-Wrong Classifier

@thm-always-wrong-pr pins down the PR curve only for $t\ge t^\star$ (a single point, via monotonicity of $\mathrm{TPR}$). The same hypothesis, applied to $\mathrm{FPR}$ instead, determines the remaining branch $t\le t^\star$ as well.

:::: {#thm-always-wrong-pr}

# PR curve for an always-wrong classifier

Suppose there exists $t^\dagger \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for $\hat{Y}_t = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t^\dagger) = 1, \qquad \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t^\dagger) = 0
$$
Then $(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t))$ traces exactly two pieces as $t$ ranges over $\mathbb R$:

- for $t\ge t^\dagger$: $\mathrm{Recall}(t)\equiv0$, $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\equiv0$
- 
- for $t\le t^\dagger$: $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\equiv1$, and $r:=\mathrm{Recall}(t)$ sweeps $[0,1]$ continuously as $t\to-\infty$, tracing
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r + \pi_0}, \qquad r\in[0,1].}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-always-wrong-pr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-always-wrong-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-always-wrong-pr .proof-content}

**Branch $t\ge t^\dagger$.** By @thm-always-wrong-pr, $\mathrm{TPR}(t^\dagger)=0$; monotonicity (@thm-roc-monotonicity) gives $\mathrm{TPR}(t)\le0$, hence $\mathrm{TPR}(t)\equiv0$ and $\mathrm{Recall}(t)\equiv0$, for every $t\ge t^\dagger$. Then $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=0$ whenever $\mathrm{FPR}(t)>0$; the convention $\mathrm{Precision}:=1$ applies only in the limit $t\to\infty$ (where $\mathrm{FPR}\to0$, @lem-roc-endpoints), never at a finite threshold. So every finite $t\ge t^\dagger$ gives $(0,0)$: the whole ray collapses to one point.

**Branch $t\le t^\dagger$.** Since $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\dagger)=1$ and $\mathrm{FPR}$ is non-increasing, $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\ge1$ for $t\le t^\dagger$, forcing $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\equiv1$ there. Substituting into @thm-precision-formula,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)+\pi_0} = \frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r+\pi_0}, \qquad r:=\mathrm{Recall}(t).
$$
As $t$ decreases from $t^\dagger$ to $-\infty$, $r=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ increases from $0$ to $1$ (@lem-roc-endpoints), sweeping the boxed curve up to $(1,\pi_1)$.

:::
::::



#### Random

:::: {#thm-random-pr}

# PR curve under random guessing

Suppose $X_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_1$, and let $\hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$. Write $p(t):=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)=\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$. Then $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ is defined if and only if $p(t)>0$, and in that case
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Recall}(t)=p(t), \qquad \mathrm{Precision}(t) = \pi_1.}
$$
Consequently the PR curve $\{(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)) : p(t)>0\}$ is contained in the horizontal line $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-random-pr-guessing')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-random-pr-guessing .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-random-pr-guessing .proof-content}

By definition, $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$ and
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\mathbb P(Y=1\mid\hat Y_t=1)=\frac{\pi_1\,\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)}{\pi_1\,\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)+\pi_0\,\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)},
$$
which is defined if and only if the denominator $\mathbb P(\hat Y_t=1)$ is positive. Since $X_0\stackrel d=X_1$, both tail probabilities equal $p(t)$, so $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=p(t)$ and the denominator equals $(\pi_1+\pi_0)\,p(t)=p(t)$. Hence $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ is defined if and only if $p(t)>0$, and then
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\frac{\pi_1\,p(t)}{p(t)}=\pi_1.
$$

:::
::::



**Interpretation.** The three cases show an asymmetry between the two ends of the PR curve.

- **$\mathrm{Recall}=1$ is the universal endpoint.** It is reached as $t\to-\infty$, where the classifier labels *everything* positive. Precision is then simply the base rate, $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$, whatever the score distributions are (@lem-roc-endpoints + @thm-precision-formula, no extra hypothesis). The perfect, random and always-wrong classifiers all pass through $(1,\pi_1)$.
- **$\mathrm{Recall}=0$ is model-dependent.** It is reached as $t\to+\infty$, where the classifier labels almost nothing positive, and $\mathrm{Precision}$ measures the purity of the *extreme upper tail* of the scores. That purity is not determined by $\pi_1$ or by the ROC endpoints alone, but by the tail ratio $\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)/\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$. The limit can take any value in $[0,1]$: $1$ for the perfect classifier (the top scores are all positives), $\pi_1$ for random guessing (the top scores carry no information), and $0$ for the always-wrong classifier (the top scores are all negatives).

This is why the earlier Gaussian and exponential derivations needed tail-rate arguments (Mills' ratio; a power-law comparison) to determine the $\mathrm{Recall}=0$ end. Unlike the $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ endpoint, it is never given for free.





##### Summary and visualization

Unlike in ROC space, none of the three transformations (threshold reversal, class label swap, and their composition) has a simple geometric description in PR space: there is no reflection or rotation of the original PR curve that produces the transformed curves. The map $(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})\mapsto(\mathrm{Recall},\mathrm{Precision})$ is nonlinear and depends on the prevalence $\pi_1=\mathbb P(Y=1)$, and each transformation also changes the role of the positive class.
Each transformed curve must therefore be recomputed from the definitions of precision and recall. Consequently, the transformed curves generally have a different shape from the original one, and, unlike the ROC curve, they all depend on $\pi_1$. What remains simple is the endpoint at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$: it is $(1,\pi_1)$ for the original curve and the threshold reversal, and $(1,1-\pi_1)$ for the two curves with swapped labels.
You can verify this directly with the interactive below.

**Interactive PR curve exploration.** The visualization below illustrates these properties for the same Gaussian model $X\mid Y=0\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, $X\mid Y=1\sim\mathcal N(1,2^2)$ as before. 
Use the **Threshold ($t$)** slider to move along the PR curve and watch the operating point change, together with the corresponding points on the transformed curves. The **Prevalence ($\pi_1$)** slider shows that, unlike the ROC curve, the PR curve and its transformations are reshaped by the class balance, and the endpoints at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ move with it. The plot also shows the threshold-reversed and class-swapped curves described above, as well as the extreme cases (perfect, random and always-wrong classifiers). ## PR curve for common distributions

Below we summarize the Precision-Recall curves for the same classic location-scale distributions as in the ROC case, along with the exponential case.
Throughout, we assume that $Z_0, Z_1$ are independent and identically distributed with a common CDF $F$ that is continuous and strictly increasing on $\{z:0<F(z)<1\}$ (this holds for every law in the table below). We define the location-scale variables as:

$$
\begin{align*}
X_0 & = \sigma_0 Z_0 + \mu_0,\\
X_1 & = \sigma_1 Z_1 + \mu_1,
\end{align*}
$$
where $\sigma_0 > 0$ and $\sigma_1 > 0$ are the scale parameters, and $\mu_0, \mu_1 \in \mathbb{R}$ are the location parameters. Unlike the ROC curve, the PR curve also depends on the prevalence $\pi_1=\mathbb P(Y=1)$, with $\pi_0=1-\pi_1$. We use the following notation:

- $\Delta = (\mu_1 - \mu_0) / \sigma_1$ (standardized separation)
- $\rho = \sigma_0 / \sigma_1 > 0$ (scale ratio)
- $\Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^z \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-u^2/2} \, du$ (standard Gaussian CDF)
- $[x]_0^1 = \max(0, \min(1, x))$ (clipping function)
- $(x)_+= \max(0,x)$

**Parametrization by recall.** Since $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-F\bigl(\tfrac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\bigr)$, the assumption on $F$ makes $\mathrm{Recall}$ a continuous, strictly decreasing bijection from $\{t:0<\mathrm{Recall}(t)<1\}$ onto $(0,1)$. Hence, for every recall level $r\in(0,1)$, there is a **unique** threshold $t_r$ with $\mathrm{Recall}(t_r)=r$, and the PR curve can be parametrized by $r$. We define
$$
G(r):=\mathrm{FPR}(t_r)=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t_r).
$$
Thus $G$ expresses the ROC curve in terms of recall: it gives the false-positive rate required to attain a given true-positive rate. Like the ROC curve, $G$ depends only on the class-conditional distributions, not on the prevalence $\pi_1$.

The endpoints $r=0$ and $r=1$ are excluded on purpose, because uniqueness may fail there. For instance, for the Uniform and Exponential laws, $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=1$ for *all* thresholds $t$ below the support, so there is no single $t_1$ and the PR curve has a vertical segment at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ (see the remark in [Appendix B](#sec-app-pr)).

Since $\mathrm{Recall}=\mathrm{TPR}=r$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=G(r)$, the PR curve is given by

$$
\mathrm{Precision}(r)
=
\frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r+\pi_0\,G(r)}
=
\Bigl(1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\frac{G(r)}{r}\Bigr)^{-1}.
$$

Consequently, the PR curve is determined by $G$ together with the class prevalence $\pi_1$. This representation will also be useful for expressing average precision as an integral over recall.



::: {style="font-size:90%; margin: 1em 0;"}
 | Law of $Z$ | CDF $F(z)$ | $G(r)=\mathrm{FPR}$ at $\mathrm{Recall}=r$ | Symmetric |
 |------------|-------------|------------------------|:---------:|
 | **Gaussian** | $\Phi(z)$ | $\Phi\bigl((\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta)/\rho\bigr)$ | ✓ |
 | **Cauchy** | $\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{\tan^{-1}z}{\pi}$ | $\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{\pi}\tan^{-1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{\tan(\pi(r - \frac{1}{2})) - \Delta}{\rho}\Bigr)$ | ✓ |
 | **Logistic** | $\dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$ | $\dfrac{r^{1/\rho}}{r^{1/\rho} + e^{\Delta/\rho}(1 - r)^{1/\rho}}$ | ✓ |
 | **Uniform** $(-\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2})$ | $\bigl[z + \tfrac{1}{2}\bigr]_0^1$ | $\Bigl[\dfrac{r-\Delta-\frac{1-\rho}{2}}{\rho}\Bigr]_0^1$ | ✓ |
 | **Gumbel** | $\exp\bigl(-e^{-z}\bigr)$ | $1 - \exp\Bigl(-e^{-\Delta/\rho}\bigl(-\ln(1 - r)\bigr)^{1/\rho}\Bigr)$ | ✗ |
 | **Exp.** | $(1 - e^{-z})_+$ | $\min\bigl(e^{-\Delta/\rho}\, r^{1/\rho},\ 1\bigr)$ | ✗ |

: FPR as a function of recall, for common distributions. The precision is $\mathrm{Precision}(r)=\bigl(1+\tfrac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\tfrac{G(r)}{r}\bigr)^{-1}$. {#tbl-distributions-pr .striped .hover}
:::


**Where the table comes from.** As for ROC, all the rows follow from a single identity (@thm-location-scale-pr): at the threshold with recall $r$,
$$
G(r)=1-F\Bigl(\frac{F^{-1}(1-r)+\Delta}{\rho}\Bigr),
$$
which simplifies to $G(r)=F\bigl((F^{-1}(r)-\Delta)/\rho\bigr)$ when $F$ is symmetric (@cor-symmetric-pr). The statements, the proofs, and the row-by-row computations are collected in [Appendix B](#sec-app-pr).

**Visualization**

The widget below lets you explore @thm-location-scale-pr interactively for the distribution described in @tbl-distributions-pr.
Use the sliders on the left to set $\mu_0,\sigma_0$ (healthy class), $\mu_1,\sigma_1$ (sick class) and the **Prevalence** $\pi_1$, and drag the **Threshold** slider to move $t$.

- The **middle panel** shows the two population densities plotted vertically: $X_1$ (sick) on the left in blue, $X_0$ (healthy) on the right in red. The horizontal black line marks the current threshold $t$; the darker-shaded region of each density is $\{X\le t\}$ (the portion of that class predicted *negative* under the rule $\hat Y_t=\mathbb 1\{X\ge t\}$) while the lighter region above the line is predicted *positive*.
- The **right panel** shows the theoretical PR curve for the current $(\mu_0,\sigma_0,\mu_1,\sigma_1,\pi_1)$, with the dashed horizontal line $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$ as the random-guessing reference (@thm-random-pr) and a marker at the operating point $(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t))$ corresponding to the threshold you've selected, so you can see exactly which point on the curve a given threshold produces, and watch the curve itself deform as you change the means, standard deviations, their ratio $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1$, or the prevalence $\pi_1$. Whatever the parameters, the curve ends at $(1,\pi_1)$ on the right.

The title above the plot reports the current $\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$, $\rho = \sigma_0/\sigma_1$ and $\pi_1$.

**PR curve for classic distributions**

:::

[Note]{.underline}: Visually, the recall is the ratio of the light blue area over the full blue area on the left, while the precision is the share of the predicted-positive mass that is blue: $\pi_1$ times the light blue fraction, divided by that quantity plus $\pi_0$ times the light red fraction.

**Interpretation**

$\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$ and $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1$ set the difficulty and shape of the underlying ROC curve, hence the function $G$; the prevalence $\pi_1$ then rescales the odds of precision.

* **Odds form:** $\dfrac{\mathrm{Precision}}{1-\mathrm{Precision}}=\dfrac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{TPR}}{\mathrm{FPR}}$. Lowering $\pi_1$ with the ROC curve fixed lowers the precision at every recall level, and the PR curve is pulled toward the horizontal axis. At fixed $(\Delta,\rho)$ the ROC curve is the same for every $\pi_1$, but the PR curve is not.
* **$\Delta=0,\ \rho=1$ (symmetric $F$):** $G(r)=r$, so $\mathrm{Precision}\equiv\pi_1$: the PR curve is the random-guessing baseline of @thm-random-pr. As in the ROC case, $\Delta=0$ alone is *not* enough when $\rho\ne1$.
* **Right end of the curve, $\mathrm{Recall}\to1$:** $\mathrm{Precision}\to\pi_1$ for every $(\Delta,\rho,F)$, which is the universal endpoint $(1,\pi_1)$.
* **Left end of the curve, $\mathrm{Recall}\to0$:** the limit is governed by the tail ratio $G(r)/r$ as $r\to0$. In the Gaussian case it is $1$ if $\rho<1$, or $\rho=1$ and $\Delta>0$; it is $\pi_1$ if $\rho=1$ and $\Delta=0$; and it is $0$ if $\rho>1$, or $\rho=1$ and $\Delta<0$. A more dispersed healthy class ($\rho>1$) therefore puts mostly healthy samples in the extreme upper tail.
* **$\Delta\to\infty$** (fixed $\rho$): $G(r)\to0$ for each $r\in(0,1)$, so $\mathrm{Precision}(r)\to1$ and the curve approaches the ideal curve through $(1,1)$.


Now we illustrate the empirical counterpart, when one samples elements from the distributions but without access to the true densities.
